content:
"Instead of consigning the branches and clippings from your winter pruning to the bonfire or shredder, turn them into a simple “dead hedge”. This natural barrier can serve as an excellent windbreak, offer shelter and habitat for a wide range of wildlife, and help define different sections of your garden. To construct one, hammer in sturdy stakes or reclaimed fence posts in two parallel lines, leaving about 50cm between them. Then weave or stack your prunings into the gap, placing the thicker, heavier branches at the bottom for stability. As you continue to add more material, it will compress and settle gradually.

If your Christmas haul was underwhelming, you might brighten your mood by pre-ordering The Book Of Seeds (Ivy Press, £30) by Paul Smith, former director of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Due out in February, this lavish volume explores 600 striking, unusual and beautiful seeds, from glossy black ones with hair-like tufts reminiscent of Donald Trump’s hairstyle to orchid seeds no bigger than a pinhead.

For planting inspiration, consider winter-flowering clematis, a real delight in the coldest months. Given a sunny and sheltered position, these climbers will produce generous displays of flowers between December and February. Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ (around 3m tall and 1.5m wide) and C. cirrhosa var. balearica (up to 2.5m x 1.5m) both bear creamy, fragrant flowers flecked with maroon, while C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ offers pure white blooms and can grow to about 5m high and 2m across. Is there anything else I can help with?"
